list.listitem: Pheochromocytomas are rare chromaffin cell tumors typically arising in the adrenal glands. C
They are characterized by excessive production of catecholamines, often leading to elevated blood pressure and symptoms of catecholamine excess. C
Plasma-free metanephrines provide the best test for excluding or confirming pheochromocytoma and should be the first test of choice for diagnosis. C
Biochemical confirmation of the diagnosis should be followed by radiologic evaluation using contrast-enhanced abdominal CT or MRI as the initial imaging to locate the tumor. C
The definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma is surgical excision of the tumor. C
All patients with pheochromocytoma must undergo pharmacologic blockade of catecholamine synthesis/effects before surgery. C
Following surgery patients should have metanephrines measured post-operatively and then annually. C

background.definition: Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-producing tumors that arise from chromaffin cells, which are neuroendocrine cells mostly situated within the adrenal medulla. Approximately 9% to 23% of tumors develop from extraadrenal chromaffin tissue (adjacent to sympathetic ganglia of the neck, mediastinum, abdomen, and pelvis) and are referred to as paragangliomas.

list.listitem: Data on the incidence of pheochromocytoma in the general population are scarce. The few published regional reports reported variable incidences, (eg, 1.55/million in Queensland, Australia).
Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma prevalance among hypertensive patients are 0.2% to 0.6% and about 3% to 7% when evaluation of incidentaloma.
Epidemiologic data showed no differences in the occurrence of pheochromocytoma between men and women.

It commonly presents between 4th and 5th decades of life P.T. Kavinga Gunawardane, A. Grossman, The clinical genetics of phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma, Arch. Endocrinol. Metab. 61 (5) (2017)490–500.

Approximately 90% of pheochromocytomas are sporadic and 10% are hereditary. A genetic susceptibility study found a truncating germline mutation on an encoding gene TMEM127 on chromosome 2q11; TMEM127 mutations were seen in approximately 30% of familial tumors and about 3% of sporadic-appearing pheochromocytomas.
Mode of inheritance: Autosomal dominant, or as a component of the multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 2 syndromes, von Hippel-Lindau disease, or neurofibromatosis.
The genetic basis of hereditary pheochromocytoma is the well-established germline mutation of the proto-oncogene RET.
Hypertension is due to the action of circulating catecholamines on cardiovascular adrenergic receptors.

The sympathetic nervous system is markedly enhanced by the loading of sympathetic vesicles with catecholamine, increased sympathetic neuronal impulse frequency, and selective desensitization of presynaptic α-2 adrenergic receptors.
Neuropeptide Y levels are increased, which has potent direct and indirect cardiovascular effects.
Norepinephrine-induced vasoconstriction is potentiated and this might be partly responsible for the hypertensive episodes.

Biochemical tests for the screening of suspected cases of pheochromocytoma include 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines, catecholamines, and vanillylmandelic acid. Plasma-free metanephrine is the best test for excluding or confirming pheochromocytoma and should be the first test of choice for diagnosis. C
Anatomical imaging studies (CT or MRI) should be combined with functional (nuclear medicine) imaging studies for optimal results to locate the tumor before surgery. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Flushing during attacks but without pallor, hypertension, palpitations, or diaphoresis
Heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, systolic hypertension
Flushing, sweating, palpitations but usually no pallor or hypertension
Likely to have a precipitating social situation

list.listitem: Certain groups of patients deserve careful evaluation. This includes patients who have episodic symptoms, panic attacks, autonomic disturbances (tachycardia, diaphoresis, especially with hypertension), a family history of pheochromocytoma, MEN-II, von Hippel-Lindau or von Recklinghausen's disease, and in any patients with incidental suprarenal or abdominal masses. About 15% of patients do not have hypertension, though.

Other situations that suggest pheochromocytoma include unexplained paroxysms of tachyarrhythmias, bradyarrhythmias, and/or hypertension during intubation; induction of anesthesia or parturition; prolonged and unexplained hypotension after an operation; and adverse cardiovascular responses to ingestion, inhalation, or injection of certain drugs, especially anesthetic agents, β-blockers, and tricyclic antidepressants.

Other conditions associated with pheochromocytoma include unexplained blood pressure variablity, difficult to control BP, previous treatment for pheochromocytoma and incidentaloma in normotensive patients.
The physical examination should of course include blood pressure measurement, and you should ask about headaches, sweating, palpitations, weight loss, and anxiety or panic attacks.

Since pheochromocytomas represent a heterogenous group of hormone-secreting tumors with variable metabolic pathways, multiple tests should be performed for best diagnostic accuracy. Accuracy varies whether the tumor is sporadic or part of a hereditary syndrome like MEN-2.

Multiple genitic mutations are suspected in certain conditions and specialized tests are available. These mutations to the VHL, NF1, RET, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC and SDHD genes have differing risks of metastatic disease or multiple tumors.

24-hour urinary metanephrines (normetanephrine and metanephrine), catecholamines (norepinephrine and epinephrine), and vanillylmandelic acid are reasonably accurate tests.Urine VMA > 40 micromole/day is the most accurate tests overall (97% sensitive, 96% specific, LR+ 24, LR- 0.03).

CT or MRI metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan are accurate for localization. A study found that higher enhancement during the arterial phase and lesion heterogeneity in a CT scan was associated with a greater likelihood of pheochromocytoma.

A recent survey demonstrated that routine non-contrast CT imaging proved useful for screening for pheochromocytoma, especially if attenuation value was less than 10 Hounsfield units and if size was less than 3 cm.

If MIBG is negative, PET or fluorodeoxyglucose(FDG)-PET may be used. In one study, 6-18F-fluoro-L-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA)-PET scanning had higher sensitivity (98% vs 53%) and specificity (100% vs 91%) than MIBG in patients with extraadrenal, predominantly noradrenaline-secreting, and hereditary types of pheochromocytoma and paragangliomas; MIBG sensitivity found here, however, is lower than previous reports. In another study, a combination of CT and 18F-DOPA-PET scanning had similar high test characteristics.
If all imaging modalities fail, and the index of suspicion is high, venous sampling from the respective adrenal veins is an option.
Differential expression of microRNA has been found between malignant and nonmalignant tumors and may help in future diagnosis and monitoring.
Consider testing for RET and VHL mutations, especially in younger patients or those with multifocal disease (based on expert opinion from Endocrine Society guidelines, clinical trials lacking).
See algorithm in .

Patients presenting with signs and symptoms (resistant or paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, perspiration, headaches) and markedly elevated metanephrines or catecholamines should undergo contrast-enhanced abdominal CT or MRI. If initial imaging is non-diagnostic, consider MRI of skull base, neck, chest and pelvis.

For patients presenting with an incidentally identified adrenal or retroperitoneal mass suspicious for pheochromocytoma (> 10 Hounsfield units on non-contrast CT), and if metanephrines are elevated, perform contrast-enhanced abdominal CT or MRI.
For patients with a large mass or extraadrenal lesions, evaluate for metastatic disease using 68Ga-DOTATATE-PET-CT or 18F-FDG-PET-CT.
The definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma is surgical excision of the tumor. C
Minimally invasive adrenalectomy is the treatment of choice for benign tumors smaller than 7 cm. C
Preoperatively, patients should undergo appropriate pharmacologic preparation, traditionally with non-selective α-blockers, phenoxybenzamine, or prazosin.C
However, calcium channel blockers have shown better clinical outcomes in a prospective study using nicardipine. B
Although a small study found no difference in outcomes with pretreatment, most experts still recommend preoperative pharmacologic preparation. C
Appropriate antihypertensive drugs (α-blockers and calcium channel blockers) are used to manage hypertension, to control associated cardiovascular symptoms, and to prepare patients for surgery.

Preoperative treatment with phenoxybenzamine (Dibenzyline) or prazosin is mainly used to counteract the sudden release of massive quantities of catecholamines during surgical intervention. In one 2-institution comparison study, there was no clinical outcome difference between use of preoperative α-blockers or phenoxybenzamine. The usual dose is phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily initially and titrated to as much as 300 mg divided twice daily.

Large prospective studies are lacking to support the efficacy of these agents. A small retrospective case series of 63 patients found no difference in outcomes with or without pharmacologic preparation. On the other hand, calcium channel blockers have been shown to suppress hypertensive crisis and are thought to inhibit catecholamine release. Nicardipine was successfully used in 10 consecutive patients with pheochromocytomas. The authors recommended that this treatment might substitute routine α-blockers in preoperative and perioperative pheochromocytoma management.
The definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma is surgical excision of the tumor, after meticulous tumor localization. Proper presurgical preparation of the patient is critical.

Alpha blockers are started 7 to 14 days before surgery and betablockers like propanalol is used to reduce heart rate closer to surgery. A systematic review of 11 studies with 1344 patients concluded that non-selective alpha blockade is preferred over selective blockade.

Minimally invasive (laparoscopic) tumor resection is becoming more popular and is recommended by the North American Neuroendocrine Tumor Society consensus guideline as the preferred treatment for primary tumors. Although randomized studies are lacking, 2 systematic reviews of 14 observational studies found better outcomes with laprascopic surgery compared with open surgery.
Malignant, metastatic, and multifocal tumors require open approaches, as appropriate.
Use of intraoperative Gallium 68 dota peptides to radiolabel tumors can identify tumors for resection.

A systematic review of 13 studies with 430 patients followed for at least 2 years concluded that the pooled recurrence rate post-operatively was 3%, with a mean time to recurrence of approximately 4 years.

A study of 242 Italian patients concluded that larger tumor size was a risk factor for both recurrence and metastatic disease. Recurrence was also more likely with younger age and with the presence of a genetic mutation.

Patients with advanced and aggressive tumors have been treated with either chemotherapy or tumor irradiation with I 131-MIBG. A systematic review found tumor response rates between 27% and 75%, with significant side effects.

A placebo controlled RCT in patients with progressing metastatic disease suggests a role for sunitinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. One year progression free survival was 36% compared to 19% in placebo arm.

A study evaluated the hypoxia-inducible factor 2α inhibitor belzutifan in 72 patients with advanced or metastatic pheochromocytoma. At 30 months, objective response occurred in 26% with disease control in 85% and progression-free survival of 22 months. On the basis of this trial the drug was FDA approved as WELIREG.
In patients with mutations in the succinate dehydrogenase subunit B gene, anti-angiogenic drugs may be effective (ie, sunitinib) but evidence is limited to animal studies and case reports.
Radiofrequency ablation of hepatic and bone metastasis has shown promise in some selected patients.
Pheochromocytomas are usually benign, but may present as or develop into a malignancy. C
Without treatment, the 5-year survival rate in metastatic disease is generally less than 50%. C

All patients with pheochromocytomas require clinical and biochemical follow-up (annually with serum or urinary metanephrins at leat for 10 years or) indefinitely, probably annually in the case of familial, extraadrenal, and right adrenal tumors, and every 2 years for patients with left adrenal tumors.C
In addition, all patients with catecholamine-secreting tumors should be offered genetic screening for familial diseases. C

In a follow-up study (median 9-years) of 36 partial adrenalectomies for pheochromocytoma among 26 patients with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, 3 patients (11%) had 5 local asymptomatic recurrences (treated with surgical extirpation or surveillance) and 3 (11%) subsequently required partial adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma on the contralateral adrenal gland. There were no malignancies.

The risk of recurrence post resection is increased in those with tumours larger than 5 cm, for whom routine follow-up imaging should be undertaken. A systematic review of 13 studies with 430 patients followed for at least 2 years concluded that the pooled recurrence rate post-operatively was 3%, with a mean time to recurrence of approximately 4 years.

A recent study of 333 patients sought to identify factors contributing to increased metastatic potential and proposed a model based on patient age, tumor size, site of pheochromocytoma and secretory status.
Pheochromocytoma is extremely rare during pregnancy, with fewer than 250 cases reported.
Diagnosis of pheochromocytoma is achieved by detecting increased catecholamines and metabolites on 24-hour urine collections. Pregnancy should not attenuate catecholamine assays.

As is the case outside pregnancy, the definitive treatment is surgery, and the laparoscopic approach is safe. The safest timing is generally thought to be either during the second trimester or as a staged procedure after a cesarean delivery. A systematic review found that found that surgery in the 2nd trimester had 2 fetal deaths out of 18 cases, compared with 2 out of 8 in the third trimester (p = NS).
Medical preparation and treatment of hypertension is essential for safe surgery.

Authors of a review of pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas noted that although most tumors are functional, tumors are increasingly identified during presymptomatic screening in children with genetic syndromes.
Although evidence is limited, management is similar to adults, including use of laparoscopic approaches.

cell.label: Evaluate for differential diagnosis of spells.
Pheochromocytoma confirmed. Consider genetic testing; preoperative preparation with (alpha/calcium channel blockers).
Reassess the diagnosis Consider functional imaging: 123 I-MIBG scan episode.
Consider unusual type of pheo or malignant pheo.
PET Scan or PET with FDG if needed.
Consider venous sampling coupled with measurement of plasma-free metanephrines.
May stop work-up here if pretest probability was low; otherwise evaluate as for mild elevation.

footnotes.footnote: Consider medications that interfere with catecholamine assays, and if feasible, stop such medications prior to testing.
Consider glucagon stimulation test, if index of suspicion is high.
If pretest index of suspicion is low, consider incidentaloma.
